translations.text: The holy gospel tells us that "reeves and sinful men drew near to the Saviour, and wished to hear his teaching.
Then the Pharisees and the scribes of the Jewish people murmured, because the Saviour received sinners and ate with them.
Then the Saviour told this parable to the Jewish scribes: "Which of you has a hundred sheep," and so on.
These words are obscure, but the commentator Gregory has revealed to us their spiritual meaning.
My dearest brothers, you have heard in this gospel reading that the sinful drew near to the Saviour's speech, and also to his table;
and the Jewish scribes found fault with that out of hatred. But their fault-finding did not come from righteousness; it came from envy. They were sick themselves, though they paid no heed to it.
Then the heavenly physician, with a gentle parable, wished kindly to heal the swelling of their hearts, and spoke thus: "Which of you has a hundred sheep,
and if he loses one of those sheep, does he not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness, and go seeking the one that he lost?"
The number one hundred is perfect, and the Almighty had a hundred sheep when the host of angels and mankind were his possessions.
But one sheep was lost to him when the first-created man, Adam, sinned and lost his dwelling in paradise.
Then the Almighty Son of God left the whole host of angels in heaven, and came to earth, and sought the one sheep that had escaped from him.
When he found it, he carried it on his shoulders to the flock, rejoicing.
When he took on our human nature and bore our sins, the straying sheep was carried back on his holy shoulders.
The lord of the sheep came home with the sheep found, because Christ, after the passion by which he redeemed mankind, rose from death and ascended rejoicing into heaven.
He called together his friends and his neighbours. His friends are the companies of angels, because in their steadfastness they continually keep his will.
They are also his neighbours, because they enjoy the glorious brightness of the sight of him in his presence.
He said, "Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost sheep." He did not say, 'Rejoice with the sheep,' but 'with me,' because our redemption is truly his joy;
and when we are led to the heavenly dwelling-place, then we will make complete the great celebration of his joy.
He said, "I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinful man, if he repents of his sins with penance, than over ninety-nine righteous who need no repentance."
We should consider this: why there is more joy over converted sinners than over innocent righteous people.
We have often seen that certain brothers who have not fallen into grave sins are not nearly so careful in practising the hard way of life, as if they were free from care,
because they have not committed the grave crimes; while certain others, who acknowledge the heavy sins they committed in their youth, are pricked with great sorrow.
They despise permitted and visible things, and with weeping they long for the invisible and heavenly things.
They despise themselves and humble themselves in all things; and because they went astray and departed from their Creator, they wish to make good the earlier loss with later gains.

There is more joy in heaven over the converted sinner, through such a way of life, than over the slothful one who trusts in himself that he has committed few and small sins, and also cares little about God's commandments and the needs of his soul.
The commander in battle has greater love for the soldier who, after fleeing, bravely overcomes his enemy than for the one who never ran away but also never did anything brave in any battle.
Just as the farmer loves the field that yields abundant crops after thorns and brambles more than he loves the one that was never thorny and does not bear fruit.
Yet there are very many righteous people who are innocent of capital sins, and who nevertheless keep as strict a way of life as if they were burdened with every sin.
No penitent can be compared to them, because they are both righteous and repentant.
From this we should consider how greatly the righteous man pleases God with humble lamentation, if the unrighteous man can please him with true penance.
The Lord then told another parable, about ten shillings, of which one was lost and was found. That parable again signifies the nine hosts of angels.

Mankind was created to make up the tenth host, because the tenth host became guilty through pride, and they were all turned into accursed devils and thrust from the heavenly bliss into the torments of hell.
Now the nine companies are named: angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominions, thrones, cherubim, seraphim.
The tenth perished. Then mankind was created to restore the lost company.
Angels are called God's messengers; archangels, high messengers; virtues, powers, through which God works many wonders.
Potestates are powers, which have power over the accursed spirits, so that they cannot tempt the hearts of faithful people as much as they wish.
Principalities are rulerships, which have charge of the good angels, and by their direction these carry out the divine mysteries.
Dominions are called lordships, because other hosts of angels obey them with great submission.
Thrones are seats of majesty, which are filled with so great a grace of the Almighty Godhead that the all-ruling God dwells in them and through them dispenses his judgements.
Cherubim means fullness of knowledge, or of understanding: they are filled with understanding so much the more, the nearer they are to their Creator through the honour of their merits.
Seraphim means "burning" or "kindling": they burn the more strongly in God's love the more closely they are joined to him;
because no other angels are between them and the Almighty God. They are burning, not in the manner of fire, but with great love of the ruling King.

The kingdom of God is filled with hosts of angels and with distinguished people, and we believe that as great a number will ascend from mankind to that heavenly kingdom as remained of holy spirits in heaven after the fall of the accursed spirits.
Nine hosts of angels remained there, and the tenth perished.
Now in turn the multitude of distinguished people will be as great as that of the steadfast angels was; and we will be ranked among their hosts according to our merits.

There are many faithful people who have little understanding to comprehend the depth of God's teaching, and yet wish, with piety, to tell other people about God's glorious works, according to the measure of their understanding:
these are ranked with the angels, that is, with God's messengers.
The chosen ones who can search out God's mysteries and preach to others with spiritual teaching are counted among the archangels, that is, the high messengers.
The saints who work miracles in this life are ranked among the heavenly Virtues, who perform God's signs.
There are also some chosen people who drive out the accursed spirits from possessed people through the power of their prayers:
to what are these ranked, if not to the heavenly powers, which subdue the hostile tempters?
The chosen ones who, through high merits, rise above the lesser brothers in authority also have their share among the heavenly principalities.
Some are so excellent that by their lordship they rule over all vices and sins in themselves, so that they are counted as gods because of that lofty purity:
of such the Almighty said to Moses, "I have appointed you to be Pharaoh's god."
These servants of God, who are of such great dignity in the sight of the Almighty that they are counted as gods,
where then does their rank fall, if not to the host that are called lordships (dominions)? For other angels are subject to them.

In some chosen people, who live with great care in this present life, the gift of God's Spirit is so great that he, sitting in their hearts as on a throne, wonderfully discerns and judges the deeds of other people.
What are these but the thrones of their Creator, in which he dwells and judges people?
True love is the fulfilment of God's law, and whoever keeps the love of God and of other people in his conduct is then rightly called cherubim;
because all wisdom and knowledge is contained in two words, that is, love of God and love of people.
Some of God's servants are kindled with such great desire to be near their Creator that they despise all worldly cares,
and with burning minds they rise above all perishable honours, and with the great burning of heavenly love they set others alight, and strengthen them with instructive speech.
What can these be called but seraphim, since through the great burning of God's love they are nearest to his presence, ahead of other earthly beings?
Now the blessed Gregory says, "Woe to the soul that passes its life without a share in the holy powers" that we have now briefly described to you.
But the soul that lacks these virtues should lament and long for the bountiful Ruler to join it, through his grace, to the lot of his chosen ones.
Not everyone receives the same gifts from God, because he grants spiritual honours to each according to his diligence.
Whoever has a lesser gift, let him not envy those who excel, because the holy hosts of the blessed angels are so ordered
that some obey others in subjection, and some are set over the others in surpassing dignity.

Great is the number of the holy spirits who dwell in God's kingdom. Of them the prophet Daniel said, "A thousand thousands served the Heavenly Ruler, and ten thousand times a hundredfold thousands stood with him."
Serving is one thing, standing with him is another. The angels who serve God are those who announce his will to the world and carry out the things that please him.
The other hosts, who stand with him, enjoy the inward contemplation of his divinity, so that they are never sent away from his presence and never leave it.
Truly, those who are sent and come to us carry out their Creator's command outwardly in such a way that they still never leave his divine joy;

for God is everywhere, though the angel is bound to a place. The Almighty Ruler is not bound to a place, because he is in every place, and wherever the place-bound angel flies, he is surrounded by God's presence.
Each host has certain gifts of its own from its Creator, yet their dignity is shared by them all, and what any one host has in part, it has fully in another host;
Of this the psalmist said, "Lord, you who sit above the cherubim, show yourself."
We said a little earlier in this reading that the throne of the Almighty was among the host that are called thrones;
but who can be blessed unless he has his Creator dwelling in himself?
Seraphim is the name of the spirits who burn with love of the Lord; and yet all the heavenly host together are set on fire with his love.
Cherubim means "fullness of knowledge" or "of understanding", and yet what angel in God's presence does not know all things?
But each of the hosts is called by the name that signifies the gift it received more perfectly.
But let us now be somewhat silent about the mysteries of the heavenly citizens, and think about ourselves, and mourn our sins in repentance, so that we,
through the Lord's mercy, may have the heavenly dwelling, as he promised us. He said in a certain place, "In my Father's house are many dwellings,"

so that if some are stronger in merits, some more righteous, and some adorned with greater holiness, none of them shall be shut out of that great house, where each receives a dwelling according to his merits.
The merciful Lord said that there would be great joy in heaven over one penitent;
But the same one said through his prophet, "If the righteous man turns from his righteousness and wickedly commits unrighteousness, I will forget all his righteousness;

and if the wicked man repents of his wickedness and practises righteousness, I will remember none of his sins." He has mercy on penitent men, but he has not promised the one who delays a sure life until the morrow.
Therefore no sinful man should delay his own conversion, lest through slackness he lose the time of God's respite.
Let every man consider his former deeds, and also his present way of life, and flee with weeping to the merciful Judge, while he waits for our amendment, he who is righteous and merciful.
Truly, the person who repents of his error is the one who does not repeat his former deeds;
of this the Saviour said to the bedridden man he had healed, "Behold, now you are healed; sin no more from now on, lest something worse happen to you."

Believers may have great trust and hope in Christ, the God who became man, who is our Protector and Judge, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.
